or investment advisor.
Ladies and gentlemen, please join me in voting.
Mr. Monich Pabrai.
For those unfamiliar, Monich Pabrai is an esteemed investor, entrepreneur, and philanthropist.
He is the founder and managing partner of Pabrai Investment Funds, a global investment firm
moving for its value or interest investment approach.
Mr. Pabrai is also a close friend of legendary investors like Warren Buffett and Charlie Munger,
and he has authored several books, including The Dundo Investor and Moziak, Perspectives
and Investing, which have become influential tax in the investment world.
And beyond his investment acumen, Mr. Pabrai is a passionate philanthropist.
He, along with his family, has established the Dakshana Foundation, which provides under-privileged
students in India with access to world-class education, empowering them to realise their
poor potential.
So please join me in giving Mr. Pabrai a warm welcome.
We will start off with an opening address by Mr. Pabrai, and we'll follow up with
questions thereafter.
All right, well, it's a pleasure to be with all of you.
Thanks for having me, and hopefully the time difference works out reasonably well.
It's not an ungodly hour on your end.
So, I just have kind of one thought I wanted to share with you guys, and then probably more
interested in what you guys want to talk about.
And in the first Gladiator movie, there's an old king who makes an appearance right at the beginning
of the movie very briefly, and that's Marcus Aurelius.
And his name comes up a few times in Gladiator 2.
But Marcus Aurelius had a very difficult life.
He spent almost his entire life on the battlefield.
Lots of injuries, lots of illnesses, lots of adversities.
And he came up with a philosophy known as the stoic philosophy, which is now the book he wrote
called Meditations, which goes over that philosophy.
But you know, the essence of what I've gotten out of it is, you know, there's a quote by him
that to encounter misfortune and overcome it is good fortune.
So basically what Marcus Aurelius is saying is that anytime we run into adversity in life,
we need to kind of, you know, man up and, you know, deal with it.
And the reward of basically dealing with it is that subsequently, that particular adversity
is going to be the kernel that leads to greater height, greater growth, etc.
And what I have found in my life, and I think, you know, Charlie Munger talks about it as well,
that basically no matter who you are, you are going to have a lot of reverses in life,
a lot of adversity, a lot of misfortune that shows up in unexpected ways.
And so it's not like some people are immune to it.
I mean, the case of Charlie, he lost his son to leukemia when the child was 11 years old.
He was very traumatic for him. There was a botched cat track operation where he lost one eye
when he was probably around 60 years old.
And then he actually subsequently had issues with the second eye as well,
where he was, there was a good chance he would go blind in that as well in blind and both eyes.
And Charlie's perspective was you always just soldier on, you know, these things are going to keep happening,
just keep moving.
And when I look back on my own life and I look at the big setbacks that came at different points
and I look back on what the impact of those setbacks setbacks was,
I cannot point to a single one that did not lead to greater growth and better outcomes in the future.
So it's, we cannot see it at the time it's happening.
We also don't know how exactly this misfortune is going to turn into a good fortune.
But my viewpoint now is that basically just have blind faith in it.
So basically if I hit some adversity, I actually now just,
I'm pretty laid back about it in the sense that I say, okay, I don't know how this is going to be helpful,
but I know it's going to be helpful.
And so I just kind of go with that.
And so far there has not been a single case where there has not been the case for me.
And in an investing context, this happened at least two times.
There were two major incidents that took place in my investing career,
which were major reverses.
The first was before, just before I had started for buy funds in kind of the 1998, 1999 timeframe,
where you know, the dot com boom was up in a big way.
The bust of 2000 had not yet come.
And there was this a big frenzy going on.
And I got carried away in that frenzy as well.
And I had invested about four and a half million dollars in a dot com startup
that would eventually go to zero.
Out of the four and a half million, about two million was my own money.
And about two and a half million was from venture capitalists and other investors and so on.
And it was just terrible.
I mean, to go through that lay off everyone and I look back, we just made so many mistakes.
But what happened with that experience was that when I later was switching to starting for buy funds
and I was going to invest in the public markets for buy funds started in July 1999.
So we were still about nine months away from the crash.
But because of my experience with dot com, I was maybe just about six to nine months ahead.
Of the public markets in terms of knowing that this was a bubble.
And it was a big bubble and was not going to end well.
And so when for buy funds started in mid 1999, I basically did not.
I mean, my background until then was all tech.
And I basically invested in almost no tech at the same time in the all these techs and dot coms are becoming very valuable or very overpriced.
Basic brick and mortar stocks in the economy were becoming very cheap.
So if you're willing to look in a more boring benign part of the market, they were great opportunities there.
And so that's kind of what a buy funds did.
And my view at that time was that the major indices, the NASDAQ, the S&P and DAW, et cetera, were not going to do well for a while.
And in fact, they could go down a lot.
And so almost the entire portfolio was anomalies.
You know, special situations and things.
And basically, I would say for buy funds in the first eight years of 99 to 2007, we had no down years.
We had around mid 30s, annualized returns before fees and probably high 20s, annualized returns after fees.
And the NASDAQ had crashed and burned and the S&P was down and the DAW was down.
So while we had climbed and done very well, all these indices, everything had gone down.
So I was by 2007, I was managing 600 odd million.
And we had made hundreds of millions in that approach.
So if I looked at the four and a half million loss and the hundreds of millions of gain, you know, it was very clear that that adversity at that time,
which was very painful, actually had a silver lining and kind of helped out and went from then.
And then this happened again in the financial crisis from 2007 to 2009, for buy funds went down like two thirds.
I mean, the markets were down about 40%.
Because we were concentrated, et cetera, we were in some just dumb mistakes.
We were down 65, 67%.
And again, basically that adversity led to a lot of rethink and some very great investments which I wouldn't have made if hadn't happened and again helped me grow as an investor.
And we did very well after 2009 as well.
So given the station in life and the position in life you're in right now where you have, you know, maybe eight decades or something ahead of you.
I think it's a very good model basically to just have this hack in your mind that whatever bad things show up or bad things happen are going to lead to good things.
And just like what Charlie says, your soldier on and those good outcomes will eventually reveal themselves.
So with that, maybe I can, you know, open up to questions and see what you guys want to talk about.
Yeah, that sounds good. We actually have some prepared questions.
And I think it's really that even that you talk about your initial experience about laws having a silver lining.
And I think it's really active on the stock market environment.
Yeah, in with deep sea AI actually causing a serious stock market correction.
You're just wondering about your perspective on it.
Do you think it's an overdue correction or do you think it's actually an opportunity to invest into the market?
I didn't get the full question. Are you talking about the current situation?
Yeah, the current situation.
The current situation I find, I mean, I think that where markets are at and what markets are likely to do usually is a fool's errand.
It's kind of not usually worth thinking too much about that.
We get to some points in time in markets where it can get obvious.
At least to some people. So for me, it was, it was obvious in 99 that this was going to end badly.
I think that was pretty obvious to me at that time.
But for example, in 2007, I was clueless about the crash that was imminent.
And, you know, pretty much just caught blindsided like a lot of other people.
And I think my current view on the market is that if I look at something like the S&P 500, I would say that probably for the next decade, maybe 10 to 15 years,
I don't think the S&P will do more than 3 to 5% a year over that period.
And now whether it goes down a lot and then kind of, you know, has robust returns after that or whether it flatlines, you know, kind of how that plays out, I have no idea.
And I'm not even sure whether my hypothesis of 3 to 5% is going to end up being inaccurate or inaccurate or whether it ends up.
I'm not particularly making bets based on that.
So the bets I'm making for the most part, I mean, so for example, I have no tech, I have nothing related to AI, for example.
And they're very basic bets there. I think they should not be correlated much with the market anyway, so the market goes up or down a flat.
I think that these businesses eventually will do as well or poorly in terms of returns as the underlying business does.
And so I think these are undervalued bets and they're good bets and sure some of them will prove we incorrect.
But I think as a basket, hopefully, will be in the right place. So that's kind of how I, and I think like for most investors, especially for all of you, I think it's not just not worth trying to figure out the market.
It's too complicated to try and do that. It's too many variables.
That makes a lot of sense. Another question that we had is that traditional value investors have had a difficult period over the years as large tech names that contributed most to the market performance.
And legends in very investing have suffered from block periods of under performance.
In given the context, do you think that investing styles should rotate or do you think value investors need to adapt to a new reality?
They take to classify investments as value or growth or things along those lines.
So all intelligent investing is value investing and it's every investment you make.
The intrinsic value of that investment is the sum of all the future cash that businesses are going to produce right now in judgment day discounted back to current dollars at some reasonable interest rate.
And so it doesn't matter whether we are talking about Nvidia or we're talking about some oil company or whether we're talking about Berkshire Hathaway.
If you have a way to figure out the cash flows of all those three different types of businesses from now to judgment day and then discounted back, it would become obvious which is the best investment.
So it's possible Nvidia could be a great value investment. It's also possible it would be could be ridiculously overvalued.
It's all a matter of what those future cash flow streams look like.
And so, you know, I mean, I think I would say what we have seen in the last few years to me at least it seems to indicate that there is plenty of euphoria amongst the large tech names, you know, the magnificent seven and so on.
And my view on those tech names is that the next maybe decade or so may not be such a great place to invest in them, but I could be wrong on that.
And whether they are a great place to invest or not depends on the cash flow streams that come out of those businesses.
So that's where the rubber meets the road.
These are very dominant franchises, extremely good management teams, huge addressable markets.
So they've got a lot of tailwinds, but at the same time, you're not investing in them at three times earnings, you know.
So to me, they fall into the two hard pile because I'm not able estimate the future cash flows of those businesses.
I don't know what Nvidia will produce in cash in 2030, for example.
And that would be a pretty critical number, try to figure out whether it's worth investing in Nvidia or not.
So basically the way I approach the problem is I limit myself to businesses where either I can clearly see what the food future cash flows are and discount those back or they fall into a category where it doesn't matter.
And mostly most of my investments fall into the matter category that it doesn't matter.
What I mean by that is that I made an investment about six years ago in a company in Turkey talked about this a few times or company in Turkey, which has a few different businesses with the main businesses leasing out warehouses, very simple business.
They're the largest kind of renter of warehouses, you know, landlord of warehouses in Turkey approximately 11 or 12 million square foot footprint.
And at the time, I had invested the day I first met them, the market cap was 16 million 16 million US dollars and I was told the liquidation value was like 600 to 800 million.
It was relatively easy to calculate the liquidation value because there were like a bunch of warehouses.
You could pretty much go to any realtor any commercial realtor in Istanbul and probably would not take them that much time to give you kind of valuations on those properties.
And there was about 200 million of debt, so the properties have probably had a value of about a billion 800 million to billion.
You take the debt out, you would like left with 600 to 800 million of equity value and your market cap is 16 million so future cash for streams of that business first of all were very predictable because they're renting warehouses and they've got leases and so one could get some view on that.
But one didn't even need to get a view on that because we were less than 3% of liquidation value.
And then I thought that we may not be able to get much stock because this might be a liquid, et cetera, but Turkey is a market filled with gamblers, the average stock at that time and maybe even today cycle through its entire float in less than 20 days.
So huge trading volumes which means that everyone was a renter of the stock, they were no real owners.
What about 8 million dollars or so we were able to get one third of the company which actually stunned me.
And at that time and even today there was a mass exodus of foreign investors leaving Turkey because the currency was so unstable and inflation was so high.
My view on that was that this is prime land and Istanbul of warehouses land and cement and concrete and steel.
All of those factors are inflation indexed.
So it doesn't really matter what the currency is, those warehouses have a value, they were kind of a global value.
So we invested and basically now that business is a market cap of over a billion US dollars.
The Turkish leader has been decimated but didn't really matter to us because I was looking at everything in dollars.
And I mean the stock has gone up 40, 50, X or whatever and it's still undervalued because now the liquidation value is north of 2 billion.
That's an example where we didn't really need to invest in really kind of figure out the cash flows.
But that business would have been relatively simple to figure out the cash flows, it wouldn't have been that hard.
I didn't bother to do it because I just said okay, it discounted to NAVS so so high that the other metric is not relevant.
What we want to do with investors is we want to reject all investments unless they fall into a category where nothing makes sense.
So when you run into investments when nothing makes sense, like I would say that our research investment when we were making it, it made no sense at all.
Why would something like that trade like that? Why would the insiders not buy in the stock? There were a lot of questions we didn't really understand.
But when things don't make sense at all and the dynamics are such that they are likely to work out in your favor, that's when you need to go all in because that won't happen very often.
So I think the experience for value investors in the last 10 years may not be that great if they were focused on kind of non tech traditional value if you will.
But as long as there, those cash flow streams are there and all of that is there, I mean markets historically have easily gone to 10, 20, 30 years of doing nothing or certain asset classes doing nothing.
So that's pretty much power for the course. So we really cannot make any any assessments of some asset class or whatever based on five or 10 years of data.
So that's how I look at it.
Right. That makes sense. I think it's a private example of a thing that you have, which is hits, I win, tails, I don't lose much.
I was just wondering on the contrary, have you ever encountered an investment where this principle has filled you and what went wrong in the instance?
Well, we have a lot of investments that don't work out in spite of our best intentions and in spite of being careful before we invest.
John Templeton used to say that the very best investment analyst is going to be wrong one out of three times.
And most of us are going to be wrong at least half the time. So if I go back and look at everything that didn't work, it's a very long list.
Of course, there is an asymmetry and the asymmetry is extremely lopsided in venture investing where when you lose money, you lose one X of what you invested.
But when you win, you might win 10,000 X of what you invested or 100 X or 1000 X.
So in that dynamic of venture investing, what is important is not so much avoiding the losers as it is to make sure the winners are in your portfolio.
I mean, that's I think that's a very difficult game. I think for me, especially I think that venture investing will be a very difficult game.
But there are some firms and some individuals who are exceptional at that game and who do really well at it.
I mean, to give you an example, I was watching a video recently with Bill Gurley who was a very successful venture capitalist at benchmark capital.
And you know, they are very focused on trying to get these 10,000 X or 1000 X in their portfolio and they've got a lot of acumen which allows them to see that.
But he said that when the Google guys came to see them and at that time, I think Google had less than 20 people on their team.
They turned down the investment. They could see many good things about it, but they also had a lot of red flags that were coming up with the Google nuances, you know, two PhD computer science students, computer science grad students who both wanted to be CEO.
They weren't interested in bringing in an outside CEO. They were hardcore nerds.
They were going to a space where there were a lot of players already Yahoo and Altavista and all that and on and on.
And so they said that it wasn't like it was close for them. He said it was a pretty much a no brainer for our partnership.
We all looked at each other and said, okay, this is an easy pass. And then he said that Sequoia and John door, both invested in Google at that time.
The pitch that Sequoia and John door heard was the same pitch that benchmark hurt.
And Bill Gurley says that they were able to somehow sift through all that data in a little bit different way than they did.
And they ended up with Google and they portfolio and they made the 10,000 and such.
So when we look at some venture capital firms, like especially let's say Sequoia capital, for example, they've shown an ability to kind of repeatedly be able to do this, you know, decade after decade.
It's quite stunning actually. They've got some DNA, magic DNA, which allows them to do that. And I think for us in the, you know, public markets, value investing world, we're not going to get 10,000 bags and 100% losses are very expensive.
So the focus has to be very heavily on trying to minimize the downside because we know we're not going to get massive.
You know, we may once in a while get something which ends up being a 10X or 20X or something, but most of the time it's going to be a game of singles.
And so when I look at a bribe fund, you know, we made a lot of mistakes during the financial crisis 2007 going into the financial crisis, I had a significant exposure to levered financial institutions.
And the worst place to be at that time. And we had a couple of zeros, you know, we took straight 100% loss on a couple of investments at that time.
And there's been plenty of losers along the way, but, you know, like Charlie used to say to me that you want to learn from your mistakes, but you don't want to learn too much.
So you have to look at your mistakes, you have to study what happened, and then you have to move on.
So it's not like we're going to get to a situation where, I mean, when I look at my portfolio today, I could not point to a particular stock that I think will not work.
But I know that as a basket, some of them will not work and then do go self-figure or become obvious which ones, but it's not obvious today.
And so that's the nature of it and that's why we need a basket and we cannot take it from there.
On that note, we'll be opening up questions to the audience. If there's anyone who has a question, please raise your hand and we'll bring the mic to you.
Thank you for taking time to speak to us today. My question is, what do you think the most overlooked principle or skill is when it comes to investing?
What do you think people aren't doing enough of now?
Well, the number one skill to be a good investor is patience and extreme patience.
So if you are the kind of person who loves to watch paint, dry, then the investing businesses for you.
And especially in public market investing, things can take many years to play out.
Even our RASAS investing, which was so extremely undervalued, did nothing for a couple of years.
I mean, to have that type of distortion in the market last for all these years is really quite remarkable.
But that's the nature of investments is that we are going to see our patience tested.
And so patience is very important. I think the second thing that's really important is that you should be able to have the thesis of your investment in three or four sentences.
Why is this investment going to work? What are drivers?
And it should be something that you should be able to explain to a 10 or 12 year old without losing them and without losing their attention span.
So it's very important to be very patient and it's very important to have extreme simplicity.
So investment ideas can be complicated, but once you've done the work, that complexity should be gone and replaced with something relatively simple.
And you know, it kind of becomes easy that way.
You know, sometimes I get asked like, okay, so this our investment in Turkey, RASAS, which is now a very large portion of the portfolio.
How did you have the conviction? Well, it's the easiest talk to have conviction in because my reference point is what's the liquidation value?
I mean, the intrinsic value is higher than that, but we haven't even gotten to liquidation value.
So when we get to a full liquidation value, then we can look at what is the intrinsic value.
So it's easy to hold the stock if it's below liquidation value.
And so the only thing I'm really, I need to really do in terms of the business is have an understanding of what liquidation values and that's it.
And so the thesis is very simple and conviction to hold it is also very simple because everything is obvious.
So if you don't have extreme clarity and extreme simplicity in your thesis, then when the stock drops 50%, which a lot of stocks will drop 50% after you buy them, you would not have the patience then to hold it because you would start second guessing all kinds of things.
But if you have a hard-coded, you know, thesis in your head, which you think is high probability.
And if that thesis is intact after the drop, the conviction state is intact as well.
So I think those are the important things as to extreme patience, coupled with extreme simplicity.
I have a question regarding your funds investment pieces and how sort of evolved over time. Do you sort of have this conviction of certain attitude invested in?
And is that still going to put you in the higher time of your fund? Or are you sort of dynamic over time and sort of decide to change some of your thesis?
My mandate gives me a lot of flexibility. I mean, the funds don't don't lever themselves. They don't go into options or derivatives. We don't short anything.
So outside of that, in terms of long, only mostly equities or all equities, it's a pretty wide mandate.
And within that mandate, there is no strategy. It's opportunistic. So we look at, you know, what makes the most sense?
What are areas of the market that are hated and unloved? For example, generally speaking, like Charlie used to say, you should go fishing where the fish are.
And so don't go fishing where all the fishermen are. Go fishing where there are no fishermen and a lot of fish. And that would be another reason to not spend too much time on the magnificent seven because there's a lot of fishermen there.
So generally speaking, you want to be where there's a lot of opportunity and no one's interested and that was the situation and that probably still is a situation in Turkey.
So that's why I decide I've been making trips every year to Turkey and we are very happy with the exposure we have there because again, it was irrational because of the extreme fear and hatred that was happening, still happening there.
Warren Buffett, I like to say has a Swami knife approach to investing. So even though Charlie monger worked on him for several decades to basically buy the great businesses and even pay up for the great businesses, which Berkshire does do.
And it's like the bulk of what they do Warren still enjoys his weird special situations and workouts and all of that. So for example, when he made the bet of the five Japanese trading companies and the way he made that bet where he borrowed the entire amount in the end, non recourse.
And the interest rate on that was half a percent a year and these stocks had a eight percent dividend yield.
So pretty much without putting up equity, he was basically significantly cash for positive after interest payments and so on. And in fact, then after that they doubled their dividends.
So in fact the yield on his investment original investment went to 15 percent just dividends, you know, and then of course the stock prices doubled as well.
So it was a huge home run, but it's because of his kind of Swami knife approach that he's able to look at a lot of things and slice and dice them a different way.
So I think as a investor being flexible reading a lot, looking at what's happening and at some point, some things may show up on the radar where you're saying, okay, this looks truly exceptional. There's no fisherman here. They seem to be a lot of fish here and it looks like a good bet.
And so then you can, you know, go for it. So that's the approach there's no strategy as such.
So I have a question more on your portfolio and how you, so I understand that you mentioned that for your individual stocks, you look at the competitive mode and the business itself, but across your whole portfolio, how do you balance across all your investment.
And I guess how do you manage risk across all your investments, considering that, you know, in very big multi-manual hedge funds now that drawdowns looked at quite closely for each portfolio.
So how do you manage across all your investment sense?
Yeah, that's a great question. And it's actually a dilemma we have faced recently in some of an extreme way. So going back to our beloved Turkish read, we own a third of the business, but 20% of that business is in one fund.
It's our offshore fund, which has about 400 odd million in assets. And so if we look at the 20% of, you know, something north of a billion more than half of that portfolio is a single Turkish stock.
And we have another stock in Turkey, which has also gone up and also become sizable. I think that's like 17 or 18% of the portfolio.
They're both very under value. So doesn't really make sense to trim those. So we are talking about like kind of more than two thirds of the portfolio and two businesses in Turkey.
Then we have in the same fund a couple of bets in the coal business, which are around 15 to 20% of assets. So by the time you, you know, look at the two Turkish businesses and the two coal businesses, you're we are already about 90 plus percent of the portfolio.
And most of my investors individual high network families, we don't have really institutions and such.
So what I told my investors is I said, look, if you have an investment in this fund and the total amount you have invested in the fund is less than one fifth of your total network.
Then if I were you, I would just do nothing just let it be because that what that would mean is that on a look through basis, no single investment in the fund is more than 10% of their network, which is pretty reasonable concentration.
And I said that if it's more than one fifth, then you should trim my recommendation that you should withdraw some of your holdings from that fund to bring it within that sort of a limit.
And, you know, invested in something on correlate. So I told them that I wasn't going to kind of adjust the portfolio.
They needed to adjust on their end, knowing what concentrations we have.
And we saw some investors act on that, which is good. And such the kind of, you know, adjusted things to kind of bring it within what they feel comfortable with.
And so we spend a lot of time now giving a lot of data and transparency to our investors on the degree of concentration and how they can mitigate some of it.
And so, you know, it doesn't make sense for us to trim something that is sitting at less than half of liquidation value that just doesn't make much sense to do, especially because good investment ideas are very rare and hard to find.
And I take the example of the Walton family, Sam Walton.
So Sam Walton, when the IPO, when Walmart had its IPO in 1970 or thereabouts, his family owned about 36% of Walmart at that time.
And he had already had that well before the IPO, he had already transferred the shares to his kids.
